z-m-13-01.title: "She drank 2/5." How many L is that?
z-m-13-01.topic: Fraction multiplication word problems: reading whether a fraction is an "amount" or a "share of the whole"
z-m-13-01.goal: Notice that the answer changes depending on whether a fraction without a unit means "that much of an amount" or "some part out of the whole," make cases yourself where the two readings differ a lot, and rewrite the sentence so it can be read only one way.
z-m-13-01.material: Sujin drank 2/5 (two fifths) of the 3/4 L (three fourths of a liter) of water that was in the water bottle. The teacher asked, "How many L of water are left?" Eunu answered 3/4 − 2/5 = 7/20 L, and Harin answered 3/4 × 3/5 = 9/20 L. The two of them read the same sentence and got different answers. (At first the bottle had only 3/4 L, and no water was added while she was drinking.)
z-m-13-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information in a problem is enough to decide one answer
z-m-13-01.thinking.1: Comparing two interpretations of one sentence
z-m-13-01.thinking.2: Making examples that fit the conditions
z-m-13-01.prereq.0: Fraction multiplication and the meaning of "some part of the whole" (grade 5 level)
z-m-13-01.s.s1.prompt: Can you decide the amount of water left from this text alone, as one answer?
z-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write one line each on what Eunu and Harin each read 2/5 as.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.hint.1: Look at what words come right after 2/5 in the text, and compare with what comes right after 3/4.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.o.a: We can decide. Multiply 3/4 by the remaining share, 3/5.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.r.a: You read 2/5 as "2/5 of the original water." First check whether the text gives a reason to read it that way.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.r.b: You read 2/5 as "2/5 L." There is no unit after 2/5, so work out whether it is okay to read it that way.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.o.c: We cannot decide. We need to know the size of the bottle.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.r.c: The size of the bottle is not used to find the amount of water left. The text says the original water is 3/4 L.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.o.d: We cannot decide. The text does not say whether 2/5 is in L or a share.
z-m-13-01.s.s1.r.d: You pointed out that the text does not say whether 2/5 is an "amount" or a "share of the original water."
z-m-13-01.s.s1.explain: There is no "L" after 2/5, so it can be read in two ways. If she drank 2/5 L, then 3/4 − 2/5 = 7/20 L is left, and if she drank 2/5 of the original water, then 3/4 × (1 − 2/5) = 3/4 × 3/5 = 9/20 L is left. Eunu and Harin each chose one reading, and within their own reading the calculation is right. To decide on one, you need to know what 2/5 is.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.prompt: You want to test both readings by letting the fraction she drank be p/q (numerator p, denominator q). Make two different p/q such that both readings ("she drank p/q L" and "she drank p/q of the original water") make sense, and the amounts left found by the two readings differ by at least 1/10 L. p/q is a fraction that cannot be reduced any further, and the denominator q is at most 12.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one p/q, find the amount left for each of the two readings, and write the difference.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.hint.1: To read it as "she drank p/q L," p/q must be less than 3/4. Within this range, change p/q and see how the difference changes.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerator and denominator are natural numbers and the denominator is at most 12.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p a natural number of at least 1 and q a natural number of at most 12.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.ok.c2: It is an irreducible fraction less than 1.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.fail.c2: It is not an irreducible fraction less than 1. The numerator must be smaller than the denominator and it must not be reducible any further.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.ok.c3: Even read as "she drank p/q L," it is less than 3/4 L, so it makes sense.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.fail.c3: If p/q is at least 3/4, it cannot be read as "she drank p/q L." She cannot drink more than 3/4 L.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The amounts left in the two readings differ by at least 1/10 L.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The difference between the amounts left in the two readings is less than 1/10 L. Change the fraction she drank, find the two amounts left, and compare the difference.
z-m-13-01.s.s2.explain: The difference between the amounts left in the two readings is (fraction she drank) × 1/4. For 2/5, it is 7/20 L and 9/20 L, a difference of 1/10 L, and for 1/2, it is 1/4 L and 3/8 L, a difference of 1/8 L. The bigger the fraction she drank, the farther apart the answers of the two readings get, and if it is 3/4 or more, it cannot be read as an "amount."
z-m-13-01.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Sujin's story in two different ways so that it can be read only one way.
z-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.0: Recall which two ways the original sentence could be read.
z-m-13-01.s.s3.hint.1: In each reading, what words could you add after 2/5 to fix the meaning?
z-m-13-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Out of 3/4 L of water, ...
z-m-13-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can each rewritten sentence be read only one way?
z-m-13-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you put into your own sentence the words that separate whether 2/5 is an "amount" or a "share"?
z-m-13-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do the two sentences show different readings?
z-m-13-01.s.s3.model.0: ① She drank 2/5 L of the 3/4 L of water. ② She drank 2/5 of the original water out of the 3/4 L of water. How many L of water are left?
z-m-13-01.s.s3.model.1: If you write that the original water was 3/4 L and she drank 2/5 L of it, it is read as an amount. Or if you write that she drank 2/5 of the original 3/4 L of water, it is read as a share.
z-m-13-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: It was written as one sentence, but each of the two readings was made.

z-m-13-02.title: The rule of changing fractions to decimals to calculate: how far is it okay?
z-m-13-02.topic: Calculations mixing fractions and decimals: when it is okay to change to decimals
z-m-13-02.goal: Judge, adjusting your confidence each time new data arrives, which fractions the rule of changing fractions to decimals gives exactly and which fractions it gives only approximately, and write that condition as a note for a younger sibling to read.
z-m-13-02.material: Seoha said, "When you calculate with fractions and decimals mixed, it is easy to change all the fractions to decimals. You can just write 1/3 as 0.33." The calculation results are revealed one by one to see how Seoha's rule does. (1/3 is read as "one third" and 5/6 as "five sixths.")
z-m-13-02.thinking.0: Adjusting your judgment and confidence as evidence grows
z-m-13-02.thinking.1: Telling apart exact values from approximate values
z-m-13-02.thinking.2: Restating a generalization by adding conditions
z-m-13-02.prereq.0: Writing fractions as decimals (grade 5 level, such as 1/4 = 0.25)
z-m-13-02.prereq.2: Rounding to the second decimal place
z-m-13-02.s.s1.prompt: The calculation results are revealed one by one. Each time, choose how to view Seoha's rule.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write the result calculated with decimals and the result calculated with fractions side by side, and mark where they are the same and where they are different.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how the digits after the decimal point end when 1/4 and 1/3 are written as decimals (whether they end or go on forever).
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.info: The first calculation is 1/4 + 0.5. Seoha changed 1/4 = 0.25 and got 0.25 + 0.5 = 0.75. Calculated with fractions, 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4, and 3/4 is 0.75.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you view Seoha's rule?
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Getting the same answer does not mean it is so for all fractions. 1/4 was a fraction that comes out exactly as 0.25. Testing with other fractions is the right next step.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The calculation results were the same, so the answer is the same for any fraction.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You went from one example all the way to "for any fraction." Think about whether there are fractions, like 1/3, that look different when changed to decimals.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: One example alone cannot tell us. Test other fractions too.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a good judgment. Having one example that is right is different from "always right," so you need to test more.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Seoha's rule is wrong. If you change a fraction to a decimal, the value changes.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Even when 1/4 was changed to 0.25, the value did not change. Work out whether there are fractions whose value changes when you change them.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Calculations mixing fractions and decimals cannot be done either way.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You can calculate by making them match, fraction with fraction or decimal with decimal. In this example, both methods were possible.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.info: The second calculation is 1/3 + 0.5. Seoha changed 1/3 = 0.33 and got 0.33 + 0.5 = 0.83. Calculated with fractions, 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6, and 5/6 written as a decimal is 0.8333… (the 3s go on forever).
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should we view Seoha's answer of 0.83?
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.after: Rounding 0.8333… to the second decimal place gives 0.83. So if the problem asks for "up to the second decimal place," Seoha's answer can be accepted. But the exact value is 5/6, and 0.83 is an approximate value a little smaller than that. You must first check what accuracy the problem wants.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 5/6 is not 0.83, so Seoha's answer is wrong in every case.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is true that 5/6 is a different number from 0.83, but if the problem asks for "up to the second decimal place," 0.83 can be the answer.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 0.83 and 0.8333… are exactly the same number, so there is no need to tell them apart.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: 0.8333… is a number where the 3s go on forever, so it is a little bigger than 0.83. They are not the same number.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: They are different as exact values, but if it is up to the second decimal place, 0.83 is also okay.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You separated exact values from approximate values and saw that it depends on the accuracy the problem asks for.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Seoha changed it to 0.33, which is the problem, so 0.33 + 0.5 cannot be calculated.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: 0.33 + 0.5 can be calculated. The problem is that the value 1/3 was changed to, 0.33, is not the exact value.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The third calculation is adding 1/3 three times. Seoha got 0.33 + 0.33 + 0.33 = 0.99. Calculated with fractions, 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 1.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What does this result tell us?
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.after: The small difference that came from writing 1/3 as 0.33 grew to 0.01 as it was added three times. The more you continue calculating, the more the difference can pile up, so if you need the exact value, it is safer to calculate with fractions as they are.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 0.99 and 1 are almost the same, so Seoha's rule is fine everywhere.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The words "almost the same" leave out how close it must be. In a problem that needs the exact value, 0.99 is not 1.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 1/3 cannot be written as a decimal, so you should not mix fractions and decimals.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: 1/3 can be written as a decimal in which the 3s go on forever. Mixing them is not forbidden in itself.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Seoha's rule has never been right so far.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: In 1/4 + 0.5, Seoha's method also gave the exact value.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Small errors keep piling up, so if you need the exact value, calculate with fractions.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You read how small errors pile up through addition and multiplication.
z-m-13-02.s.s1.reflect: Did Seoha's rule seem right at first? As the examples grew one by one, which thoughts changed and which stayed the same? What can you look at to tell whether you need the exact value or an approximate value is enough?
z-m-13-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to tell your younger sibling about Seoha's method. Write a short note, with fraction examples, saying when it is okay to use this method and when to be careful.
z-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.0: See whether you can use the way 1/4 and 1/3 look as decimals as evidence in your note.
z-m-13-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try writing it in two parts: "It's okay when..." and "Be careful when...".
z-m-13-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does the note say both "when it's okay" and "when to be careful"?
z-m-13-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Do the fraction examples you gave support what you said?
z-m-13-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you separate the cases where you need the exact value from the cases where an approximate value is enough?
z-m-13-02.s.s2.model.0: A fraction that comes out exactly as a decimal, like 1/4 or 1/5, is still exact if you change it to a decimal to calculate. But 1/3 is 0.333… going on forever, so writing 0.33 is an estimate. If you need the exact value, calculate with fractions.
z-m-13-02.s.s2.model.1: If the problem only asks for the second decimal place, you can write 1/3 as 0.33. But if you add 0.33 three times you get 0.99, which is not 1, so when you keep calculating, be careful that errors pile up.

z-m-13-03.title: 3/4 L of water, 1/6 L bottles: which story fits?
z-m-13-03.topic: Fraction division: choosing a story that fits the expression and making cases where it fills with nothing left over
z-m-13-03.goal: Tell whether a story matches fraction ÷ fraction meaning "how many times one amount fits in another," make cases yourself where it fills with nothing left over, and when the quotient is a fraction, read the actual number of bottles to fit the question.
z-m-13-03.material: Seoyeon wants to make a story that fits the fraction division 3/4 ÷ 1/6. There may be just one story or several that fit the same expression. First you will pick the right one among four stories, and then you will make a story yourself.
z-m-13-03.thinking.0: Choosing a situation that fits the meaning of the expression
z-m-13-03.thinking.1: Making several cases that fit the conditions
z-m-13-03.thinking.2: Reading the value of the quotient and the actual number needed as different things
z-m-13-03.prereq.0: Experience of thinking of division as "how many times one amount fits in another"
z-m-13-03.prereq.1: The meaning of fractions and irreducible fractions (grade 5 level)
z-m-13-03.s.s1.prompt: Seoyeon wants to make a story that fits 3/4 ÷ 1/6. Which story has the value of this expression as its answer? (3/4 is three fourths, and 1/6 is one sixth.)
z-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each story, write what amount 3/4 and 1/6 each stand for.
z-m-13-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check one by one whether the story asks how many times 1/6 fits in 3/4.
z-m-13-03.s.s1.o.a: When 6 people share 3/4 L of water equally, one person's share
z-m-13-03.s.s1.r.a: This is a story about dividing water equally by 6 (3/4 ÷ 6). 1/6 is not the number of people but the amount in one bottle.
z-m-13-03.s.s1.o.b: When you drink 1/6 of 3/4 L of water, the amount you drank
z-m-13-03.s.s1.r.b: This is a story asking how much 1/6 of 3/4 is (3/4 × 1/6). It does not ask how many times 1/6 fits in 3/4.
z-m-13-03.s.s1.o.c: When you pour 3/4 L of water into 1/6 L bottles, the number of bottles
z-m-13-03.s.s1.o.d: When you combine 3/4 L of water and 1/6 L of water, the total amount
z-m-13-03.s.s1.r.d: This is a story about combining two amounts (3/4 + 1/6). It does not ask how many times one amount fits in another.
z-m-13-03.s.s1.explain: The story that asks how many times 1/6 L fits in 3/4 L fits 3/4 ÷ 1/6. The value is 9/2, that is, 4 and 1/2. Division can be shown by two kinds of stories, "sharing equally" (partitive) and "how many times one amount fits in another" (quotative), and since the 1/6 in this expression is the amount in one bottle, not the number of people, the second kind of story fits.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.prompt: This time, make a story like Seoyeon. You want to fill 1/c L bottles (c is the denominator of one bottle) completely with n/d L of water (numerator n, denominator d), with nothing left over. The water is an irreducible fraction less than 1 L, d is at most 12, and c is a natural number from 2 to 12. You need at least 2 bottles. Make three different cases.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.0: Choose an amount of water, change the size of the bottle, and count how many times the amount in one bottle fits in the water.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.hint.1: 3/4 L and 1/6 L did not fill the bottles completely. See what bottle size would fit exactly.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c1: n, d, and c are natural numbers in the proper ranges.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make n a natural number of at least 1, d at most 12, and c from 2 to 12.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c2: The water is an irreducible fraction less than 1 L.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The amount of water n/d is not an irreducible fraction less than 1 L.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.ok.c3: It fills the bottles completely with nothing left over.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c3: There is water left over. Count how many times 1/c fits in the amount of water and check whether it is a natural number.
z-m-13-03.s.s2.fail.c4: One bottle is enough. Try making the bottle smaller (make c bigger).
z-m-13-03.s.s2.explain: The number of times 1/c fits in the amount of water n/d is n×c÷d. This value must be a natural number for the bottles to be filled completely. For example, 3/4 L in 1/4 L bottles is 3 bottles, 2/3 L in 1/3 L bottles is 2 bottles, and 1/2 L in 1/6 L bottles is 3 bottles. 3/4 L in 1/6 L bottles is 4 bottles and a half bottle, so it does not fill them completely.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.prompt: 3/4 ÷ 1/6 = 9/2, that is, 4 and 1/2. You want to pour all of the 3/4 L of water into 1/6 L bottles. A bottle that is only half full is still counted as one bottle. At least how many bottles are needed?
z-m-13-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write in words what the 4 and the 1/2 in the quotient 4 and 1/2 each mean for the bottles.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find out whether there is water left after filling, and work out whether another bottle is needed for that water.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.r.b: 4 counts only the full bottles. You need one more bottle for the leftover 1/12 L of water.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.r.c: A bottle is something you cannot cut into pieces. You must think separately about the value of the number (the quotient) and the actual number of bottles needed.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.r.d: 9 is the numerator of the quotient 9/2. You have to read the fraction as 4 and 1/2 and then decide the number of bottles.
z-m-13-03.s.s3.explain: The quotient 4 and 1/2 means 4 full bottles and a half bottle more. The water left is 3/4 − 4×1/6 = 1/12 L (the amount for half a bottle), and a bottle is needed for that too, so there are 5 bottles in all. If the question asks "how many bottles are full," it is 4, and if it asks "how many bottles are needed," it is 5. The same quotient is read differently depending on the question.

z-m-13-04.title: What if the information changes in a copied expression?
z-m-13-04.topic: Expressions mixing fraction multiplication and division: order of calculation and changed information
z-m-13-04.goal: Tell apart the order of calculation (left to right when there are no parentheses) from how reliable a copied expression is, adjust your judgment and confidence each time new information arrives, and make cases yourself where the value changes with the order.
z-m-13-04.material: Minho copied a homework problem into his notebook. The answer key has one answer written on it, but it is covered and cannot be seen. The information below is revealed one piece at a time. (3/4 is read as three fourths, 3/8 as three eighths, and 2/5 as two fifths.)
z-m-13-04.thinking.0: Revising your judgment or adjusting your confidence according to new information
z-m-13-04.thinking.1: Working out what information is needed
z-m-13-04.thinking.2: Making counterexamples where the value changes with the order
z-m-13-04.prereq.1: The agreement that in an expression mixing multiplication and division, you calculate from the left when there are no parentheses (grade 5 level)
z-m-13-04.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, choose what you think the answer on the answer key is.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate the copied expression in order from the left, calculate the expression with parentheses separately too, and compare the values.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether the new information changes the "expression," or leaves the expression as it is and changes only "how much you believe it."
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.info: Minho copied a homework problem into his notebook. The copied expression is 3/4 ÷ 3/8 × 2/5 and has no parentheses. The answer key has either 4/5 or 5 written on it, but it is covered and cannot be seen.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which side is the answer on the answer key more likely to be?
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.after: If you calculate the expression without parentheses as it is, 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 2 and 2 × 2/5 = 4/5. On the other hand, it has not yet been checked whether the copied expression is the same as the original. Both the judgment that it is 4/5 and the judgment that it cannot be decided yet are reasonable at this point.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 5: because you must do the multiplication first
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: When multiplication and division are mixed and there are no parentheses, you do not do the multiplication first; you calculate in order from the left.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 4/5: because with no parentheses you calculate in order from the left
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You calculated the copied expression as it is. If nothing changed while copying, this is a fitting judgment.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: We cannot tell: the parentheses may have been dropped while copying
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You worked out that there is no guarantee that the copied expression is the same as the original. This judgment points out what information is needed.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Neither: because you can only calculate fraction division after changing it to multiplication
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even if you change it to multiplication, the order of calculation does not change. You can calculate from the left with the changed expression too.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Minho said, "Thinking back, I think the back part, 3/8 × 2/5, was grouped with parentheses in the original problem. But I'm not sure."
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, which side is the answer on the answer key more likely to be?
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If it is an expression with parentheses, you calculate 3/8 × 2/5 = 3/20 first, and then 3/4 ÷ 3/20 = 5. But Minho's memory is not certain. You may lean toward 5, but it is too early to be sure, and checking the original problem is the most reliable method.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 4/5: the copied expression has no parentheses, so take it as it is
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It has not been confirmed that the copied expression is the same as the original. Think about how to take Minho's new memory into account as evidence.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 5: decide that Minho's memory is right
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Minho himself said he is not sure. A memory is evidence, but it is not grounds for being sure.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 5 seems more likely but it is not certain, so check the original
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You took the new evidence into account while adjusting how confident you are.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: We cannot decide yet. Both cases remain.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This judgment says that even with the new memory, it has not been confirmed. It is reasonable until you see the original.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Minho found the original problem in his notebook. The original expression is 3/4 ÷ 3/8 ÷ 2/5 and there were no parentheses. Minho copied the last ÷ wrongly as ×.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the value of the original expression 3/4 ÷ 3/8 ÷ 2/5 calculated in order from the left?
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 2 and 2 ÷ 2/5 = 5. It was right that there were no parentheses, but what was wrong was the × that was copied. The first judgment of 4/5 was right for the copied expression and not right for the answer key. The judgment that it could not yet be decided was reasonable until this fact came out.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: It is the value you get when you read ÷ as ×, or when you calculate the back part 3/8 ÷ 2/5 first. Check what happens when you calculate in order from the left.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You calculated only up to 3/4 ÷ 3/8 and stopped. You must divide that quotient 2 by 2/5 one more time.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You calculated only the back part 3/8 ÷ 2/5. The first division by 3/4 is missing.
z-m-13-04.s.s1.reflect: How did your first judgment (it is 4/5, or it cannot be decided) change each time you saw new information? Which information changed your judgment, and which information changed only how confident you were? What could you do to reduce mistakes when copying?
z-m-13-04.s.s2.prompt: You want to test with the copied expression written as 3/4 ÷ 3/8 × p/q. Make two p/q such that the value calculated in order from the left and the value when you calculate the later 3/8 × p/q first are different. (p and q are natural numbers from 1 to 20, and count fractions with the same value only once.)
z-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose one p/q and find the value calculated from the left and the value when the later part is calculated first.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.hint.1: If there is a p/q where the values came out equal, look at what shape it has, and choose again avoiding that shape.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p and q natural numbers from 1 to 20.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of the two calculations are different.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The values of the two calculations are the same. Change p/q and find the two values and compare them.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.explain: Calculating from the left, 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 2 and 2 × p/q = 2p/q. If you do the later product first, 3/4 ÷ (3/8 × p/q) = 2q/p. The two values are the same only when p = q, that is, p/q = 1. For example, if p/q = 2/5, they differ: 4/5 and 5.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.prompt: In 3/4 ÷ 3/8 × p/q, what kind of number is p/q when the values of the two calculations become equal? Use the numbers of the examples you tested at least once, and write your guess.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you find both values in the examples you gave and compare them?
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you test with other examples whether there is only one case where they become equal?
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.model.0: They are the same only when p/q is 1. If you put in 2/2 or 3/3, both values come out as 2. If you put in 2/5 or 3/4, they differ, like 4/5 and 5.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.model.1: The two calculations were the same only when the numerator and denominator were the same, that is, for a fraction with value 1. 2/5 and 3/4 were different.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.hint.0: Put various fractions into p/q, and organize into a table in two columns which ones make the two calculations give the same value and which make them differ.
z-m-13-04.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the fractions that came out the same with those that came out different, and look for a form they share.

z-m-13-05.title: Splitting up before dividing: which way works?
z-m-13-05.topic: Dividing mixed numbers: can you split either number up to calculate?
z-m-13-05.goal: Compare two ways of splitting mixed numbers to calculate, using the evidence in a table, tell apart what the examples show from what they do not show, and explain why one method works and why the other does not.
z-m-13-05.material:
Gaon and Narae described ways of splitting up to calculate division of mixed numbers.
Gaon: "Split the mixed number being divided into its whole-number part and fraction part, divide each by the divisor, then add."
Narae: "I split the divisor, the mixed number, into its whole-number part and fraction part, divide the number being divided by each, then add."
These are the results of the two of them trying their own methods on two problems. (2 1/2 is read as "two and one half" and 12 1/2 as "twelve and one half.")
Problem / Exact value / Gaon's method / Narae's method
2 1/2 ÷ 1 1/4 / 2 / 2 / 12 1/2
3 1/3 ÷ 1 2/3 / 2 / 2 / 8 1/3
(The exact values were found by changing both mixed numbers to improper fractions.)
z-m-13-05.thinking.1: Telling apart the power of a counterexample from the limits of examples
z-m-13-05.prereq.0: Writing mixed numbers as improper fractions, fraction division (grade 6 level)
z-m-13-05.prereq.1: The case where adding quotients gives the quotient of the sum (e.g., 6÷3 + 3÷3 = 9÷3)
z-m-13-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything you can say with evidence from the table.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the "Exact value" column of the table with each method's column side by side, and mark where they are the same and where they differ.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, tell apart whether it states "what was seen in the table" or states a bigger conclusion than what was seen in the table.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.o.a: Narae's method was not right in either problem, so we can be sure it is never right for any mixed number.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.r.a: Two examples let us say only that "this method always works" is broken. To say "it is never right," we would have to look at more cases.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.o.b: Gaon's method was right in both problems, but this alone does not let us be sure it works for all mixed numbers.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.r.b: The fact that examples were right and the statement "always right" are different. You did not miss that difference.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.o.c: Both methods split up, divide, and add, so they are the same method.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.r.c: What is split is different. Gaon split the number being divided, and Narae split the divisor.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.o.d: Narae's method was not right in two problems, so the statement "it always works" is broken.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.r.d: You used the fact that one counterexample breaks "always."
z-m-13-05.s.s1.o.e: Gaon's method was right in two problems, so we can be sure it works for all mixed numbers.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.r.e: Even with several right examples, you cannot be sure about "all." You need a reason why it works.
z-m-13-05.s.s1.explain: Narae's method was different from the exact value 2 in both examples, so the statement "it always works" is broken. But this table alone cannot confirm "it never works in any case." Gaon's method was right in two examples, but being right in examples does not mean it works in every case. You have to work out the reason.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.prompt: To say that Gaon's method works for all mixed numbers, what more evidence would be needed besides the two examples in the table?
z-m-13-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the case where you keep the divisor as it is and split only the number being divided, with the case where you split the divisor.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.o.a: Make a few more examples with bigger numbers and count whether Gaon's method is right.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.r.a: Even with more examples, "all" is not confirmed. Examples only make a belief stronger.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.o.b: Narae's method is wrong, so Gaon's method must be right.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.r.b: A method being wrong does not make the other method right. You must work out Gaon's method separately.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.o.c: Work out why the sum of the quotients of the split parts equals the quotient of the whole.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.o.d: Ask the teacher whether Gaon's method is right.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.r.d: It would be confirmed, but it is different from working out for yourself why.
z-m-13-05.s.s2.explain: If you split the number being divided and add the quotients from dividing each part by the same number, it equals the quotient of dividing the whole by that number from the start. For example, 6 ÷ 3 + 3 ÷ 3 = 9 ÷ 3. This reason is the same whether or not the divisor is a mixed number, so Gaon's method can be used in all cases. On the other hand, if you split the divisor, this reason does not hold.
z-m-13-05.s.s3.prompt: Explain why Narae's method is not right, using the numbers from the table at least once.
z-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the value from Narae's method and the exact value side by side in the table and compare which is bigger and by how much.
z-m-13-05.s.s3.hint.1: Look at how each of the two quotients that were added in Narae's method compares with the exact value.
z-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you compare using the numbers taken from the table?
z-m-13-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain in your own words why splitting the divisor makes the result big?
z-m-13-05.s.s3.model.0: With Narae's method, 2 1/2 ÷ 1 1/4 becomes 12 1/2, but the real value is 2. This is because when you split the divisor into 1 and 1/4 and add the quotients from dividing by each, the quotient gets too big.
z-m-13-05.s.s3.model.1: In 3 1/3 ÷ 1 2/3, Narae's method gives 8 1/3 and the real value is 2. If you divide separately by 1 and 2/3, each quotient is already big, and when you add them it cannot be right.

z-m-13-06.title: If 5 people share 2 cakes, how many pieces does each person get?
z-m-13-06.topic: Writing the quotient of a whole-number division as a fraction: amount and number of pieces
z-m-13-06.goal: Tell apart that the quotient of a division of whole numbers can be written as a fraction (an amount) and that to say it in pieces, you need to know more about how to cut, find the cases that divide with nothing left over, and think of different ways to solve the cases that do not.
z-m-13-06.material: Somi's group of 5 people wants to share 2 cakes of the same size equally. Each cake can be cut into equal-sized pieces, and how many pieces to cut it into has not been decided yet. The teacher asked, "How many pieces will each person eat?" Somi answered, "2 ÷ 5 = 2/5 (two fifths), so it is 2/5 of a piece."
z-m-13-06.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
z-m-13-06.thinking.1: Finding several values that fit the conditions
z-m-13-06.thinking.2: Thinking of several ways to solve it
z-m-13-06.prereq.0: Writing the quotient of whole number ÷ whole number as a fraction (grade 5 level, 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5)
z-m-13-06.prereq.1: Quotient and remainder of division (grade 3-4 level)
z-m-13-06.s.s1.prompt: What is a fitting thing to say about Somi's answer "2/5 of a piece"? (The 2 cakes are the same size and each can be cut into equal-sized pieces. How many pieces to cut it into has not been decided yet.)
z-m-13-06.s.s1.hint.0: For the case of cutting one cake into 5 pieces and the case of cutting it into 10 pieces, find the number of pieces one person eats in each.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check in the text whether the "2/5" in Somi's answer is the number of "pieces" or the "amount of cake."
z-m-13-06.s.s1.o.a: It is right. 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5, so one person eats 2/5 of a piece.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.r.a: 2/5 is a number that shows the amount of cake. The size of a piece depends on how it is cut, so you cannot say "2/5 of a piece."
z-m-13-06.s.s1.o.b: 2/5 is the amount of cake, and the number of pieces depends on how it is cut.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.o.c: We cannot decide. We need to know the weight of one cake.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.r.c: The weight is not needed to find the amount of cake one person eats (2/5 of a cake).
z-m-13-06.s.s1.o.d: We cannot decide. We need to know how many cakes there are.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.r.d: The information that there are 2 cakes is already given. Look again for what information is still unknown.
z-m-13-06.s.s1.explain: 2 ÷ 5 = 2/5 means that one person eats 2/5 of a cake. To say "how many pieces," you need to know how many pieces one cake is cut into. For example, if one cake is cut into 5 pieces, one person eats 2 pieces, and if one cake is cut into 10 pieces, one person eats 4 pieces. Even for the same 2/5 of a cake, the number of pieces changes depending on how it is cut.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.prompt: You want to cut each cake into s equal pieces. For the pieces of the 2 cakes to be shared by 5 people in equal numbers with no pieces left over, into how many pieces must one cake be cut? The number of pieces s is a natural number from 2 to 12. Find two different values of s.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.hint.0: Choose an s, find the total number of pieces, and check whether there are pieces left over when 5 people share equally.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.hint.1: Look at whether the s values you found have anything in common.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.var.s: Number of pieces s in one cake
z-m-13-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of pieces is a natural number from 2 to 12.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make s a natural number from 2 to 12.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The total pieces are shared equally by 5 people with no pieces left over.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.fail.c2: Pieces are left over or short. Check whether the total number of pieces is divisible by 5.
z-m-13-06.s.s2.explain: If you cut the 2 cakes into s pieces each, there are 2×s pieces in all. For 5 people to share equally with no pieces left over, 2×s must be divisible by 5. If s = 5, 10 pieces are divided into 2 pieces each, and if s = 10, 20 pieces are divided into 4 pieces each. Up to 12 pieces, these are the only two.
z-m-13-06.s.s3.prompt: Say the cake was cut into 8 pieces per cake. Then it is hard for 5 people to eat the same number of pieces with no pieces left over. Write different ways you could make them eat equally.
z-m-13-06.s.s3.hint.0: Find the total number of pieces and write the quotient and the leftover pieces when 5 people share.
z-m-13-06.s.s3.hint.1: Think of two or more ways to handle the leftover pieces so that everyone gets the same amount.
z-m-13-06.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., The total number of pieces is ..., if each person takes ... pieces, ... pieces are left. So ...
z-m-13-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find and write the total number of pieces and the number of pieces one person gets?
z-m-13-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your way of handling the leftover pieces fit the condition that everyone eats the same amount?
z-m-13-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think of two or more different ways?
z-m-13-06.s.s3.model.0: If 5 people share 16 pieces, each person gets 3 pieces and 1 piece is left. If you cut the leftover 1 piece into 5 smaller pieces and give one to each person, everyone ends up the same.
z-m-13-06.s.s3.model.1: If each person gets 3 pieces, that is 15 pieces and 1 piece is left over, so you cannot share equally. Either nobody eats the leftover piece and it is kept, or you cut one cake into 5 or 10 pieces from the start.

z-m-13-07.title: Raon's calculation trick: how far does it work?
z-m-13-07.topic: Decimal multiplication: seeing the decimal you multiply by as a fraction and changing to division
z-m-13-07.goal: Explain, using the relationship between decimals and fractions, why the method of changing multiplication by a decimal into division works, find the decimals it works for, and test cases where it does not work with numbers to decide the range of the generalization.
z-m-13-07.material: Raon calculated 7.2 × 0.25 like this. "0.25 is 1/4, so I can just divide 7.2 by 4. 7.2 ÷ 4 = 1.8!" When 7.2 × 0.25 was actually calculated in vertical form, it was also 1.8. Raon said excitedly, "I bet any multiplication by a decimal can be changed to division like this!" (7.2 is read as "seven point two" and 0.25 as "zero point two five.")
z-m-13-07.thinking.0: Explaining why a calculation method is right
z-m-13-07.thinking.1: Making examples that fit the conditions
z-m-13-07.thinking.2: Testing a generalization and deciding its range
z-m-13-07.prereq.1: Writing decimals as fractions (0.25 = 1/4, grade 5 level)
z-m-13-07.prereq.2: The relationship between finding 1/4 of a number and dividing it by 4
z-m-13-07.s.s1.prompt: What is a fitting reason that calculating 7.2 × 0.25 as 7.2 ÷ 4 gave the same value?
z-m-13-07.s.s1.hint.1: 1/4 of 7.2 is one of how many equal parts of 7.2?
z-m-13-07.s.s1.o.a: The two values just happened to be the same when calculated.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.r.a: It is not a coincidence. There is a reason connecting multiplying by 0.25 and dividing by 4.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.o.b: Division is easier than multiplication, so it is okay to do it that way.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.r.b: Being easy is a reason for choosing a method, not a reason the values are the same.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.o.c: Because 0.25 is a number with two decimal places, so you can divide by 4.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.r.c: Not every number with two decimal places can be turned into division by some number. You have to look at the nature of the number 0.25 itself.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.o.d: 0.25 is 1/4, and multiplying by 1/4 is the same as dividing by 4.
z-m-13-07.s.s1.explain: 0.25 = 25/100 = 1/4. 1/4 of a number is one part when the number is divided equally by 4, so multiplying by 1/4 and dividing by 4 are the same. 7.2 × 0.25 = 1.8 and 7.2 ÷ 4 = 1.8.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.prompt: Find decimals c for which Raon's method (seeing the decimal you multiply by as 1/k, and dividing by k) works. c is a number greater than 0 and less than 1 with up to two decimal places, and 1/c is a natural number. Find three different values of c.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.ok.c1: c is greater than 0 and less than 1.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.fail.c1: c must be greater than 0 and less than 1.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.ok.c2: c is a number with up to two decimal places.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.fail.c2: Please make c a number with up to two decimal places. (like 0.25)
z-m-13-07.s.s2.ok.c3: c is of the form 1/k (k is a natural number).
z-m-13-07.s.s2.fail.c3: 1/c is not a natural number. Check whether c, when changed to a fraction, has a numerator of 1.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.explain: If c written as a fraction has a numerator of 1 (1/k), multiplying by it can be changed to dividing by k. Among numbers with up to two decimal places, there are 0.5 (=1/2), 0.25 (=1/4), 0.2 (=1/5), 0.1 (=1/10), 0.05 (=1/20), 0.04 (=1/25), 0.02 (=1/50), and 0.01 (=1/100).
z-m-13-07.s.s3.prompt: Raon said, "I bet any multiplication by a decimal can be changed to division like this!" Test the case of multiplying by 0.3 with 7.2, and write what you would say to Raon.
z-m-13-07.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate 7.2 × 0.3 and 7.2 ÷ 3 and write them side by side.
z-m-13-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write 0.3 as a fraction and compare it with 0.25 = 1/4.
z-m-13-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both values you calculated (the product and the quotient)?
z-m-13-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why 0.3 written as a fraction is different from dividing by 3?
z-m-13-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also say for which decimals Raon's method works?
z-m-13-07.s.s3.model.0: 7.2 × 0.3 = 2.16 but 7.2 ÷ 3 = 2.4, so they are different. 0.3 is not 1/3 but 3/10, so the method does not work for every decimal.
z-m-13-07.s.s3.model.1: 0.3 is 3/10. Dividing 7.2 by 3 gives 2.4, but 7.2 × 0.3 is 2.16, so they are not the same. It works only for decimals that equal a fraction with numerator 1, like 1/4 and 1/5.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the decimal you multiply by as a fraction and see whether the numerator becomes 1.
z-m-13-07.s.s2.hint.1: Write a few decimals as fractions and sort them into those where the numerator becomes 1 and those where it does not.

z-m-13-08.title: Testing Gaon's "method you use only when it divides evenly"
z-m-13-08.topic: Fraction division: the range in which the method of finding a common denominator and dividing the numerators works
z-m-13-08.goal: Test the claim that the method of finding a common denominator and dividing the numerators can be used "only when it divides evenly" with a counterexample, and say why this method can be used in any case.
z-m-13-08.material: When dividing fractions, there is a method of finding a common denominator for the two fractions and then dividing the numerators. For example, 4/5 ÷ 2/5 has the same denominator, so it is 4 ÷ 2 = 2. While using this method, Gaon said, "The method of finding a common denominator and dividing the numerators can be used only when the numerators divide evenly. If they don't divide evenly, you must not use this method." (4/5 is read as four fifths and 2/5 as two fifths.)
z-m-13-08.thinking.0: Judging what kind of example can break a claim
z-m-13-08.prereq.0: Finding a common denominator of fractions (grade 5 level)
z-m-13-08.prereq.1: Changing fraction division into multiplication (grade 6 level)
z-m-13-08.prereq.2: Division of fractions with the same denominator (e.g., 4/5 ÷ 2/5)
z-m-13-08.s.s1.prompt: What kind of example would help most to test whether Gaon's statement is right?
z-m-13-08.s.s1.explain: Gaon's statement is "it can be used only when it divides evenly." If this statement is wrong, there should be examples where the common denominator method's answer is right even when it does not divide evenly. So finding such examples and comparing them with the value from multiplying by the reciprocal helps the most.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.prompt: Make two different divisions a/b ÷ c/d where, after finding a common denominator, the numerators do not divide evenly (the remainder of dividing the numerators is not 0). Both fractions are irreducible fractions less than 1, the denominators are at most 12, and the two denominators are different. Find the common denominator using the least common multiple of the two denominators.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.var.a: Numerator of the first fraction a
z-m-13-08.s.s2.var.b: Denominator of the first fraction b
z-m-13-08.s.s2.var.c: Numerator of the second fraction c
z-m-13-08.s.s2.var.d: Denominator of the second fraction d
z-m-13-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The numerators and denominators are proper natural numbers.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the numerators at least 1 and the denominators natural numbers of at most 12.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.ok.c2: Both fractions are irreducible fractions less than 1.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c2: Both fractions must be irreducible fractions less than 1.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c3: The two denominators are the same. Please make the denominators different so that a common denominator is needed.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.ok.c4: The numerators after finding the common denominator do not divide evenly.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.fail.c4: The numerators after finding the common denominator divide evenly. Find the common denominator, get the two numerators, divide, and change to fractions that leave a remainder.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.explain: For example, finding a common denominator for 5/6 ÷ 1/3 gives 5/6 ÷ 2/6, and 5 ÷ 2 does not divide evenly but is 5/2. It is the same as 5/6 × 3 = 5/2, found by multiplying by the reciprocal. 2/3 ÷ 3/4 is 8/12 ÷ 9/12, so 8 ÷ 9 = 8/9, and it is the same as 2/3 × 4/3 = 8/9. After finding a common denominator, the denominators are the same, so the quotient of the numerators equals the quotient of the two fractions, and if it does not divide evenly, you can write the quotient as a fraction.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.prompt: What would you like to say to Gaon? Using the numbers from the examples you made above, write how Gaon's statement should be corrected.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the examples you made above and write side by side the value from dividing the numerators after finding the common denominator and the value from multiplying by the reciprocal.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how to change "only when" in Gaon's statement to make it a true statement.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your example, did you check that the value from dividing the numerators after finding the common denominator and the value from multiplying by the reciprocal are the same?
z-m-13-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also say how to write the quotient when it does not divide evenly?
z-m-13-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you say in one sentence how Gaon's statement should be corrected?
z-m-13-08.s.s3.model.0: You can use it even when the quotient of the numerators after finding the common denominator does not divide evenly, like 5÷2. Finding a common denominator for 5/6 ÷ 1/3 gives 5/6 ÷ 2/6, and 5÷2=5/2. It is the same as 5/6×3=5/2, found by multiplying by the reciprocal.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.model.1: It doesn't matter if it doesn't divide evenly. You can just write the quotient as a fraction. 1/2 ÷ 3/4 is 2/4 ÷ 3/4, so 2÷3=2/3, and it is the same as 1/2×4/3=2/3.
z-m-13-08.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite in one sentence the case in which Gaon's statement says not to use this method.
z-m-13-08.s.s1.hint.1: For each choice, consider what kind of example is needed to show that statement is wrong.
z-m-13-08.s.s1.o.a: Recalculate a few divisions with the method of multiplying by the reciprocal and check whether that method is right
z-m-13-08.s.s1.r.a: The method of multiplying by the reciprocal is a method you already know. It does not test Gaon's statement.
z-m-13-08.s.s1.o.b: Choose a division that does not come out even and test whether the value found by the common-denominator method is right
z-m-13-08.s.s1.o.c: Choose only divisions of fractions that have the same denominator and test whether the method is right
z-m-13-08.s.s1.r.c: Fractions with the same denominator need no common denominator. You have to look at cases that need a common denominator.
z-m-13-08.s.s1.o.d: Collect more divisions where the numerators divide evenly and check whether the method is right
z-m-13-08.s.s1.r.d: Even if more examples that divide evenly come up, they cannot break the statement "only when it divides evenly." That statement is about the cases that do not divide evenly.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.hint.0: First choose two denominators and find the least common multiple. Then convert the two fractions to that denominator and find the two numerators.
z-m-13-08.s.s2.hint.1: Divide the first numerator by the second numerator, calculate directly to check that the remainder is not 0, and if it is, change the fractions.
z-m-13-08.s.s3.model.2: 1/2÷1/3=3/6÷2/6=3÷2. Even if it does not divide evenly, you can write the quotient as the fraction 3/2, so you can use this method.
